title: Health and exercise-related medical issues among 1,212 ultramarathon runners: baseline findings from the Ultrarunners Longitudinal TRAcking (ULTRA) Study
population: 1,212 active ultramarathon runners (ULTRA Study enrollment data, retrospective self-report)
findings: 64.6% reported an exercise-related injury in the preceding year that resulted in lost training days (median 14 days); the knee was the most common injury site.
Prior-year stress fracture incidence was 5.5%, most (44.5%) in the foot; stress fractures were more common in women than men (p < 0.01).
Runners with exercise-related injuries were younger (p < 0.001) and less experienced (p < 0.01) than those without injury.
The most prevalent chronic conditions were allergies/hay fever (25.1%) and exercise-induced asthma (13.0%); serious conditions (e.g. coronary artery disease 0.7%) were uncommon.
limitations: Retrospective self-report from a convenience cohort; prevalence over one year, not a prospective injury-incidence study; no training-load variables in the abstract.
implications: Treat younger and less experienced ultrarunners as higher injury risk in progression logic: use conservative ramp rates and an explicit injury-history check.
Expect a median of about 2 weeks of lost training in a typical injury year when sizing buffer weeks in a long build (descriptive only).
Add a bone-stress caution (foot) in plans for women, without a numeric threshold.

verification.notes: Added in this review as an essential ULTRA Study paper named in the topic scope. Crossref (2014-01-08, first author Hoffman, PLoS ONE) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 24416176) fetched; all numbers stated in the abstract.
